meta.title: The potential adverse effects of hypodermic glucagon-like peptide -1 receptor agonist on patients with type 2 diabetes: A population-based study.
meta.abstract:
Background

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), a class of injectable antidiabetic drugs, have shown significant efficacies in improving glycemic and weight control in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the long-term safety of GLP-1 RAs remains insufficiently studied. This study aimed to provide real-world evidence on potential adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use in T2D patients without major chronic diseases including impaired cardiac or renal function.

Methods

We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 7746 T2D patients on GLP-1 RAs in Shenzhen, China. They were compared with 124 371 metformin-only users and 36 146 insulin-only users, forming two therapy control groups. GLP-1 RAs users were also further 1:2 paired with the control groups. Competing risk survival analyses were conducted to assess the incidence risks, presenting subdistributional hazard ratios (sHRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for various adverse outcomes associated with GLP-1 RAs use.

Results

Compared with metformin-only users, GLP-1 RAs use was associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes (sHRs with 95% CIs), including pancreatitis (2.01, 1.24-3.24), acute nephritis (3.20, 2.17-4.70), kidney failure (3.73, 2.74-5.08), thyroid cancer (2.25, 1.23-4.10), and thyroid dysfunction (1.27, 1.00-1.63), respectively; Similar results were also found when compared with insulin-only users. Importantly, long-term (≥12 months) GLP-1 RAs use may further elevate the incidence risks of pancreatitis, acute nephritis, thyroid cancer, and thyroid dysfunction.

Conclusion

Compared with traditional T2D treatments, GLP-1 RAs use may be associated with increased risks of various adverse outcomes in a Chinese population. Cautions were strongly warranted in the use of GLP-1 RAs. Further validation is crucial across diverse populations.

domains.name: Confounding
domains.direction_justification: GLP-1 RA users had significantly higher baseline socioeconomic status (citizen health insurance: 75.60% vs 54.96% in metformin; undergraduate education: 26.07% vs 11.94% in metformin) and higher baseline obesity rates (BMI 30-39.9: 13.21% vs 4.87% in metformin, Table 3S). Furthermore, critical clinical confounders were virtually unmeasured (HbA1c was missing in 91.27% of patients and FPG missing in 33.22%, Table 1 footnote). Matching was performed on missingness dummy categories (e.g., 'Unspecified' BMI comprised 32.49% to 36.08%), leaving massive residual confounding by indication and surveillance.

findings.title: Uncontrolled confounding by disease severity and metabolic control
findings.mechanism: Key prognostic determinants of renal, pancreatic, and neoplastic outcomes—specifically HbA1c (missing in 91.27%) and diabetes duration—were not controlled for. Patients prescribed second-/third-line GLP-1 RAs inherently differ in glycemic severity and disease progression compared to metformin monotherapy users.

domains.name: Selection of participants into the study
domains.direction_justification: Out of 985,278 initial diabetes outpatients, 177,381 were excluded for missing IDs and 362,035 (36.7%) were excluded for missing prescription data (Figure 1), creating a highly selected subset whose follow-up and capture in the health registry may be systematically related to both treatment choice and diagnostic recording.

findings.title: Massive attrition due to missing records and IDs
findings.mechanism: Over 54% of the initial eligible cohort was discarded due to administrative missingness (missing IDs and missing prescription history), potentially introducing selection bias if record completeness correlates with healthcare seeking and adverse event recording.

domains.name: Post-exposure interventions
domains.direction_justification: Patients were defined as monotherapy users if cumulative duration of other antidiabetic medications was <6 months, permitting co-medication changes during follow-up that could independently affect renal or metabolic endpoints.

findings.title: Permissible multi-drug treatment up to 6 months
findings.mechanism: Allowance of up to 6 months of concurrent antidiabetic agents introduces potential post-baseline co-intervention effects on adverse event profiles.
evidence: Accumulative prescription period of any other antidiabetic medication <6 months allowed

domains.name: Missing data
domains.direction_justification: HbA1c was missing in 91.27% of the cohort, FPG was missing in 33.22%, and primary demographic variables (BMI, Education, Marital Status) had missing rates exceeding 32% (Table 1, Table 3S). Patients with complete records were more likely to have frequent clinical encounters and active diagnostic workup.

findings.title: Pervasive missingness in biological and clinical parameters
findings.mechanism: With >90% missing HbA1c and >32% missing BMI, adjustment models cannot adequately condition on the primary markers of disease severity and obesity.
evidence: HbA1c missing rate: 91.27%
FPG missing rate: 33.22%
BMI unspecified: 32.49% to 36.08%

domains.name: Measurement of the outcome
domains.direction_justification: Patients initiated on novel, expensive injectable therapies (GLP-1 RAs) undergo heightened clinical monitoring, ultrasound surveillance, and laboratory testing compared to routine metformin users, inflating the detection rate of subclinical or diagnostic outcomes such as thyroid cancer (sHR 2.25) and thyroid dysfunction (sHR 1.27).

findings.title: Surveillance and diagnostic detection bias
findings.mechanism: Outcomes were identified via ICD-10 codes and regex matches from outpatient/hospital records without adjudication. Enhanced clinical contact for injectable therapy increases the probability of incidental diagnosis of thyroid nodules/cancer and asymptomatic renal laboratory abnormalities.
evidence: Table 2S: Regular expression and ICD-10 matching on unadjudicated outpatient/inpatient text
Reported sHR of 2.25 for thyroid cancer and 15.09 for leukemia

domains.name: Selection of the reported result
domains.direction_justification: The authors performed exploratory outcome-wide scanning across dozens of organ systems (pancreatitis, thyroid cancer, skin follicular cysts, leukemia, acne, etc.) without pre-registered statistical analysis plans or corrections for multiplicity, amplifying false-positive associations.

findings.title: Outcome-wide exploratory scanning without multiplicity correction
findings.mechanism: Testing multiple ICD-10 disease categories across various duration cutoffs (<12 vs ≥12 months) and drug subclasses without family-wise error rate control leads to selective reporting of nominally significant extreme effect estimates (e.g., leukemia sHR 15.09).
evidence: Over 18 distinct adverse disease categories evaluated across multiple stratified models
Significant findings reported selectively without pre-specified trial registry protocol

overall.summary: This retrospective database study is at very high overall risk of bias under ROBINS-E. The findings of elevated risks across numerous heterogeneous conditions (e.g., acute nephritis sHR 3.20, renal failure sHR 3.73, thyroid cancer sHR 2.25, leukemia sHR 15.09) are largely driven by massive residual confounding, severe missing data (HbA1c missing in 91.27%, BMI missing in >32%), propensity score matching on missingness categories, substantial surveillance/detection bias for injectable therapies, and uncorrected multiplicity in exploratory scanning.

unresolvable_without_more_data: Raw event counts for each adverse outcome per treatment arm to compute absolute risk differences and numbers needed to harm
Complete baseline glycemic control (HbA1c, fasting glucose) and diabetes duration data for >90% of the cohort to assess residual confounding by indication
Data on clinical visit and surveillance frequency between GLP-1 RA and oral metformin users to quantify detection bias for indolent outcomes (e.g., thyroid cancer)

baseline_comparability.summary: At baseline, GLP-1 RA users were younger but substantially more obese (BMI 30–39.9 kg/m²: 13.21% vs 3.04% in insulin and 4.87% in metformin) with higher citizen health insurance coverage and higher post-match HbA1c. These imbalances in obesity, glycemic control, and surveillance favor the control groups and push hazard ratio estimates for adverse outcomes away from the null.

time_related_biases.summary: The study defines exposure retrospectively across total follow-up, introducing immortal time and selection bias by conditioning on future treatments. Furthermore, the absence of a lag period for oncologic outcomes with short mean follow-up (23.7 months) inflates apparent harms via detection and protopathic bias.
